prompt: Items (weight, value): (3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 6), weight limit 10. The 0/1 version (capacity loop downwards) returns 11. You switch to the unbounded version, with the capacity loop running **upwards**. What does it return, and why?

options.text: 13: it can reuse the 3 kg item, and 3 + 3 + 4 fills 10 kg exactly
options.explanation: Correct. Allowing copies opens packings the 0/1 version can't use. Two 3 kg items and one 4 kg item weigh 10 kg and are worth 4 + 4 + 5 = 13.

options.text: 11: loop direction only matters when an item has a duplicate in the list
options.explanation: Loop direction matters for every item: upwards, `best[c - w]` may already include the item, so it can be used again. 11 (4 kg + 5 kg) is the 0/1 answer.
12 is a valid unbounded packing, but 3 + 3 + 4 fills the same 10 kg for 13.

options.text: 16: four 3 kg items, because 3 kg has the best value per kilogram
options.explanation: Four 3 kg items weigh 12 kg, over the limit. The best ratio alone does not decide the packing.

workedExample:
1. Upwards, `best[c - w]` may already include copies of the current item, so each item can be reused. That is exactly unbounded knapsack.
2. Compare sensible fillings of 10 kg: 3+3+3 (9 kg) is worth 12; 3+3+4 (10 kg) is worth 13; 5+5 is worth 12; 4+4 and 3+5 (8 kg) are worth 10.
3. The best is 13. The DP table for limits 0 to 10 ends `..., 10, 12, 13`, choosing the best possible last item at each limit.
4. Value per kilogram favours the 3 kg item (about 1.33), but three of them waste 1 kg; replacing one with a 4 kg item uses it. Again, a ratio rule is not enough for whole items.
